source.title: Towards Understanding Generalization of Deep Learning: Perspective of Loss Landscapes
source.authors: Lei Wu; Zhan-Xing Zhu; E. Weinan

record.tranche_reason: Compares optimization and batch conditions and measures loss-landscape properties against held-out performance, using methods distinct from the claim versions' cited studies.
record.gate_note: The paper's attack-set experiments deliberately create poorly generalizing solutions; they do not train on fixed random labels. The initialization results and polynomial-fitting example do not compare a claim-version condition. Table 1 compares full-batch and mini-batch gradient training; Table 3/Figure 3 relate Hessian-based proxies to test accuracy.
record.test_reason: Table 1 directly compares held-out performance under full-batch and mini-batch training, bearing on V5's batch-size component. The epoch budgets are unspecified, so it does not establish the fixed-budget claim. The Hessian experiments do not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: they argue that good minima have larger attraction basins and that this explains why random initialization usually reaches good solutions. They provide a restricted two-layer theoretical analysis and deeper-network numerical evidence, while acknowledging that their Hessian proxies are rough. These results do not establish magnitude-aware sharpness or directly measure global basin volumes.
record.recipe_differences: Uses attack-set construction of poor-generalizing minima and Hessian eigenvalue/Frobenius-norm proxies; the batch comparison uses full-batch gradient descent versus mini-batch SGD. These are not the original versions' procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The batch comparison varies full-batch versus mini-batch training; landscape measurements vary dataset and network. Hessian-based proxy has reported variance and limited ability to distinguish equal generalization performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Across attack-constructed and ordinary solutions with approximately perfect training accuracy, better test accuracy is associated with smaller unscaled Hessian proxies, with substantial variability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unscaled Hessian curvature can distinguish broadly different generalization performance among these constructed solutions.

record.problems: The basin-volume measures are acknowledged as rough proxies; the reported relationship has variance and cannot distinguish minima with equivalent generalization performance. Figure 3 reports the landscape comparisons graphically without numeric values in the text. The batch comparison does not state that epochs or training schedules are held fixed.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Initialization-strategy results and the attack-set construction are not claim-version results; cited results from other studies are not extracted.

untested.parts: No paired natural-label and fixed random-label experiments measuring training fit and held-out accuracy.
No width sweep beyond the width required for zero training error.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive versus nonadaptive optimizer comparison with specified tuning.
Equal epoch budgets, workload-dependent batch thresholds, language models, and remedies involving longer training or adapted recipes are not tested or established.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbation tolerance and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures are not tested.
No removal and retraining comparison involving highly memorized versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Table 2's fixed epoch counts apply to initialization experiments and cannot be transferred to Table 1. Failure to distinguish minima with equivalent generalization performance is not itself a failure to rank different generalization gaps.

versions.untested_parts: No fixed random-label training or comparison of random-label and natural-label test performance.
No width sweep past the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.

The full-batch versus mini-batch comparison bears on batch size, but the text does not state that this comparison uses a fixed epoch budget, a workload-dependent threshold, or adaptive recipe changes.
The paper measures Hessian-based landscape proxies, not magnitude-aware weight perturbations or the ranking against norm- and margin-based measures specified in the version.

rows.subject: mLeNet
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch gradient descent versus mini-batch SGD on MNIST.

conditions.value: MNIST; first 10,000 images used for training

rows.note: Mini-batch SGD has higher test accuracy than full-batch training.
rows.check: The direction was misclassified: full-batch accuracy is 0.77 percentage points lower, consistent with a large-batch penalty. The table labels full batch as 10^5, but Section 3.1 specifies only 10,000 training examples; flag this source inconsistency. Epoch budgets are unreported.

rows.subject: mLeNet
rows.operation_detail: Related test accuracy to the sum of logarithms of the top 50 Hessian eigenvalues, used as an inverse-basin-volume proxy.

conditions.value: 512 examples; remaining training examples used as attack set

rows.measure: Test accuracy versus Hessian eigenvalue proxy
rows.value: Good minima have larger valleys than bad minima; the relation shows variance and the proxy barely distinguishes minima with equivalent generalization performance.
rows.note: The text describes the trend and its limitations but gives no numeric values for this plotted comparison.
rows.check: Unscaled Hessian eigenvalues do not measure V7's tolerance to magnitude-scaled weight perturbations. Much of the performance range is deliberately constructed using incorrectly labeled attack data.

relationships.condition: mLeNet and sNIN on 10,000 MNIST training examples; epoch budgets unspecified
relationships.reason: R1 and R3 show full-batch accuracy below mini-batch accuracy by 0.77 and 1.52 percentage points, respectively; this supports the batch-size component without establishing the fixed-epoch condition.
relationships.display_finding: The study's comparisons suggest lower full-batch accuracy for mLeNet and sNIN, without establishing equal epoch budgets. These comparisons have not been verified.

relationships.condition: LeNet on 10,000 MNIST training examples; epoch budgets unspecified
relationships.reason: R2 shows essentially equal accuracy, 97.85% versus 97.87%, so this comparison shows no material batch penalty; it is not an established fixed-budget counterexample.
relationships.display_finding: The study reports essentially equal LeNet accuracies across batches, but the comparison remains unverified and does not establish matched training budgets.
